extracted.intended_audience: AI researchers, ML practitioners, product designers, and researchers interested in LLM evaluation and computational humor
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how well large language models understand, generate, and adapt humor — including linguistic, cultural, creative, and safety aspects — as a benchmark of model sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory (humor by surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The incongruity theory posits that humor emerges from the unexpected — it's the surprise element when our brains predict one outcome and something entirely different ensues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incongruity as an evaluative dimension: does the generated joke create a perceptible, context-appropriate surprise? Examples/notes: the article cites Martin (2007) and frames unexpectedness as central to many jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory (humor from feeling superior)
rubrics_metrics.description: The superiority theory suggests that humor stems from a sense of superiority over others — we laugh at others' blunders or misfortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the model can craft or recognize humor that rests on social hierarchical cues or mockery, and whether it handles such material appropriately (ethical/safety concerns may apply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory (humor as tension release)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relief theory views humor as a release of pent-up tension — a well-timed joke can diffuse stressful situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether generated humor serves a tension-diffusing social function and whether the model times or frames such humor recognizably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of humor types
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor comes in many flavors — slapstick, satire, dark humor, wordplay, puns, sarcasm — each with unique characteristics and appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmark performance across multiple humor types rather than one: can the model produce/recognize slapstick vs satire vs dark humor vs puns and adapt style appropriately?

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependence and cultural sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is highly context-dependent and culturally-rich; a joke funny in one culture may fail in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cross-cultural appropriateness and the model's ability to use context to select culturally-relevant references; test on culturally diverse prompts and measure failures where humor misfires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Models often produce well-known jokes rather than original material — they are not hard coded but not original either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure novelty: does the model produce original, non-memorized jokes? Use prompts that prevent relying on common jokes (e.g., highly specific or curveball prompts) and check for repeats of canonical jokes (Jentzsch & Kersting, 2023).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity and ability to make surprising connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity is the ability to surprise, subvert expectations, and connect seemingly unrelated ideas to produce amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether outputs show genuine, surprising conceptual connections rather than pattern-matched recombinations. The article argues LLMs primarily perform pattern recognition rather than true creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic timing, intonation, and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often depends on timing, intonation, and delivery — elements not fully captured in raw text training data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether textual outputs imply effective timing/delivery (pauses, punchline placement) and recognize that lacking audio/performative cues limits some humorous effects (e.g., scripts alone won't convey Seinfeld timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic nuance: wordplay, puns, irony, satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often relies on linguistic nuances such as wordplay, puns, sarcasm, and irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test specific linguistic phenomena (puns, double entendres, sarcasm detection/generation). Cite prior computational work (Taylor & Mazlack, 2004) as relevant benchmarks for wordplay recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and social understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor reflects human emotions and social dynamics; effective humor requires grasping these 'unspoken' aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the model demonstrates awareness of social context, emotional tone, and interpersonal dynamics necessary for appropriate humor; deficits here limit resonance and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety, offensiveness, and censorship constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often walks a fine line between amusing and offensive; LLMs are often governed by strict censorship guidelines and may avoid edgy humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how models navigate sensitive content: do they avoid offense at the cost of humor, or do they produce inappropriate content? Consider safety filters and policies as part of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and diversity of training data
rubrics_metrics.description: The data used for training needs to be diverse and representative of different cultures, languages, and contexts to capture the broad spectrum of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess dataset coverage: are many humor styles, languages, and cultures represented? Poor representation will bias what humor the model can generate/understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of annotated datasets for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated datasets, with examples of humor labeled by structure, content, and context, are crucial for training models to recognize and generate humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the presence and richness of annotations (structure, intent, audience reaction) and use them to train/test recognition and generation tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability and evolution over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor evolves with societal norms and trends; models must be updated to remain relevant and sensitive to current social context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how models incorporate fresh cultural references and adjust to changing norms; evaluate need/frequency of retraining or continual learning to keep humor current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity of humor and benchmarking difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is highly subjective, making it difficult to establish a universal standard for evaluating humor across different LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multi-annotator, demographic-diverse human evaluations and accept variance; prefer comparative and relative benchmarks rather than single absolute scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to produce diverse, non-repetitive variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating many variations of jokes is not the same as producing genuinely different or funnier jokes; often many variations are 'just more of the same'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure diversity of comedic ideas, not just token-level variation. Use prompts that require distinct comedic strategies and evaluate whether multiple outputs are meaningfully different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical consistency versus humor effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Models may produce answers with logical consistency but little actual humor; funniness is not guaranteed by coherence alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate funniness separately from grammaticality/coherence; include human rating scales for humor impact rather than relying on automated fluency scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility in applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical applications of humor — customer service, entertainment, marketing — require that humor enhances engagement, defuses tension, or increases memorability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess downstream metrics (engagement, satisfaction, conflict de-escalation, campaign recall) when deploying humor-capable systems in real-world settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization and presence of lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Human humor often derives richness from personal experiences and emotions; LLMs lack lived experience, reducing depth and resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate personalization ability (tailoring jokes to user profile) and whether the model can simulate personal-feeling humor without crossing into inauthentic or deceptive territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation methodology: curveball and constrained prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Using unique requirements (e.g., 'single funniest joke about 3-toed sloths') prevents reliance on memorized jokes and can reveal creativity gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In testing, include curveball/specialized prompts that constrain or force novelty; the article provides examples of sloth prompts used to probe originality and variety across models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal relevance and trend awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often reflects current societal norms, trends, and events; relevance changes over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the model's humor references are timely and whether it can incorporate or avoid dated references; consider updating data to match current events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of linguistic proficiency via humor tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: An LLM's ability to create or interpret humor can be seen as an indicator of its linguistic proficiency and understanding of social dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include humor tasks as part of broader linguistic benchmarks to measure nuanced language understanding, irony detection, and pragmatic inference.
